entry.title: King Ghidorah Is Ready for Its Close-Up: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Cracked the Legendary Monster’s Next Evolution
entry.summary: 'Godzilla Minus Zero' poducer Kazuaki Kishida and visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima on the detail work that makes King Ghidorah such a threat.
entry.content:
“Godzilla Minus Zero” builds on the strong visual foundation — and/or the rubble of Tokyo’s Ginza district — that director Takashi Yamazaki pounded into his previous film, “Godzilla Minus One.” Like that first film, “Minus Zero” is in conversation with the big ideas and cultural/emotional resonances behind Toho’s giant monsters, and it’s attuned to the beloved visual details of the franchise, going all the way back to the original “Godzilla” and the Shōwa era.

But historically, for all kinds of budgetary and technological reasons, King Ghidorah is usually not ready for his close-up.

The amount of time that “Godzilla Minus Zero” spends with its three-headed mutant space dragon on the ground is a notable departure from how Ghidorah is most often depicted: in flight, or towering far above Godzilla. Even in closer shots in a CGI-rich film like “Godzilla: King of the Monsters,” when all three heads get ready to chomp up a puny human or 10, the emphasis is on Ghidorah’s scale. Three heads are more terrifying than one.

Related Stories
Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It?
From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race

But “Godzilla Minus Zero” spends a lot of time with just one head, or focused on just one head, and its Ghidorah is as scary on the ground as it is in the air, and this is in part due to the particular design experience that director Yamazaki and his team brought to the world’s deadliest gold dragon. Yamazaki was tapped to design “Godzilla the Ride” at Seibuen Amusement Park (its full name is Godzilla the Ride: Giant Monsters Ultimate Battle) in 2021 and therefore had to figure out a version of Ghidorah that would work from the other side of a safety rail.

Yamazaki and animation studio Shirogumi worked on a monster concept that would feel, according to “Minus One” and “Minus Zero” producer Kazuaki Kishida, “as though the audience was under attack by Ghidorah itself. So it had to be very scary and very close-up,” Kishida told IndieWire. “[In the ride,] we see Ghidorah basically crawling on the ground with its neck, because it has a very long neck, and then really going after the audience. To bring King Ghidorah very close to humans and bring the eyeline closer was a huge core concept for this. So there was a lot of research that had gone into the ride that we were able to apply to ‘Godzilla Minus Zero.'”

The film uses Ghidorah’s eyeline to great effect. One of the most unnerving moments in its initial attack on Matsumoto City, as scientists Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka) and Akira Hagiwara (Ko Maehara) scramble to both document the new monster on the block and survive the utter destruction of whole city blocks, is a moment of getting really, uncomfortably close to Ghidorah’s eye.

That forced proximity to Ghidorah makes all the spectacular space-dragon stuff it can do even more effective, though these effects are also as grounded in the natural and the tangible as much as possible. For Ghidorah’s destructive beam, for instance, visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima did more research than even he thought he could do on how lightning visualizes itself.

“Everyone sort of recognized the string of light, that line of light. But if you look at lightning in slow motion, it leaves a line of something that lingers — this is apparently just water vaporizing instantly and turning into plasma,” Nojima told IndieWire. “I don’t fully know the science behind it, but there’s a visual effect that lightning leaves behind. So for Ghidorah’s destruction beam, I wanted to emphasize that element of it. I scatter particles around, kind of blur the imagery, and then let it linger longer than it normally would.”

Of course, whenever the destruction beam hits something, Nojima and the VFX team got to build the explosion. But it’s that visual sense of Ghidorah’s power lingering, and of getting too close to where Ghidorah can see you, that makes this version of the monster feel so dangerous.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now playing in theaters.

entry.title: Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’
entry.summary: Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore on singing, emulating Patti LuPone and Liza Minnelli's haircut, and embracing comedy for "The Debut."
entry.content:
“Hello, I’m Julie,” said a radiant Julianne Moore, holding out her hand as she popped out of the elevator at Middleburg, Virginia’s Salamander Resort. Her hair was red, her skin was white, her dress as yellow as gold. A few hours later after a rapturous Middleburg Film Festival reaction to “The Debut” (December 11), we talked in a hotel meeting room. The A24 crowdpleaser has been wowing audiences and critics since Telluride.

Jesse Eisenberg has done it again. His follow-up to “A Real Pain,” which won Kieran Culkin the Supporting Actor Oscar, could score Best Actress for Moore. The musical comedy has earned Moore raves on the festival circuit for her role as a sad suburban homemaker turned anxious aspiring actress in a New Jersey community theater. A sixth Oscar nomination is inevitable, and possibly a second Oscar win after “Still Alice” in 2015. It’s hard to believe she launched her career in 1988 as a regular on soap opera “As the World Turns.”

Related Stories
Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It?
From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race

Moore is the current Best Actress frontrunner, even though she has won before. Sometimes nabbing an Oscar is a disadvantage in the Oscar race. But not if the performance is undeniable: Katharine Hepburn holds the record with four, while nipping at her heels are three-time winners Meryl Streep, Frances McDormand, Jack Nicholson, and Sean Penn.

Eisenberg wrote a rich character for Moore, knowing what the veteran actress could do with the childlike housewife Mona who, in order to learn how to act, must find herself. The director and actress had worked together on “When You Finish Saving the World” (2022). “[‘The Debut‘] is about this woman who has been chewed up but not spit out,” said Eisenberg, quoting Mona’s signature song. “It’s my point of view through somebody I consider a muse. I was writing something about myself as a seven-year-old in 1990, but I couldn’t picture anybody else except her doing it.”

It helped that Moore had told Eisenberg exactly what she was looking for. “I said I had just done ‘Dear Evan Hansen,’ and I loved singing, and I would love to have another opportunity,” she said. “I told him that I would love to do more comedy, and I didn’t want to play some suffering mom.”

Eisenberg put all of this in the screenplay, “but in the most surprising and inventive way,” she said. “He’s such a specific writer. He’s so incredibly empathetic. He has a compassionate worldview. He understands creativity. All of that stuff went into this wonderful and delightful story. It’s joyful and life-affirming too.”

Moore didn’t know she was playing a seven-year-old version of Eisenberg until he started telling that to the press. “Then he was like, ‘This is my experience of being a kid and going to community theater.’ But I could sense that there was a personal point of view in it. I very much felt with Mona that she was on a subjective journey, and that he was inside of that. With Mona, I always knew he was looking through her.”

“The Debut” is told from her point of view, as she tries to talk the overbearing local community theater director Jerry (Paul Giamatti) into hiring her, an untrained actress. He does it because he has no one else. But first, he must teach her how to act.

Mona dresses like a schoolgirl, with skirts, blouses, cardigan sweaters. “She’s so contained, and the way she learns is so literal,” said Moore, “the way a baby learns, like, you make a face at a baby, the baby makes a face back, but they don’t have intention behind it. But they’re learning things in an exterior way, and then they match it with feeling later on. So everything she’s doing is a childlike way of learning.”

Mona goes from an invisible nonentity in her own home to someone who demands attention. “She’s a kid who has found friends for the first time,” said Eisenberg. “She’s the girl who transferred to the right school at seven years old, and then the first rehearsal happens, and she is told she is terrible, and she has no idea why. And it’s the girl who transferred to the right school and gets an F on the very first test, and then the rest of the semester is panicking, and all she’s seeing is everybody else get A’s, and she still has the F, and she doesn’t know what to do. And then the teacher pulls her aside and says, ‘You either show up, or you are out on your ass.’ And something switches in her, and she makes the decision: ‘I am going to show up.’ And she begins to turn into a monster.”

The theater troupe embraces Mona as she unfolds like a flower. “We’ve been like those theater kids cracking corny jokes and finding community,” said Moore. “It’s all done with so much affection. Jesse looks at that world with not a hint of malice.”

Giamatti’s director relentlessly pushes the newbie through her paces until they have a powerful confrontation on the empty stage where he forces her to break down. Eisenberg reduced the actors’ anxiety by placing the eight-page showstopper in the middle of the shoot: not the beginning, and not the end. On the first day he went over to Moore’s apartment to talk about the movie. He said, “I really don’t want you to worry about that scene. I don’t want you to worry about memorizing that because I know that as an actor, I would I lose my mind. I would just be drilling it all the time, and I wouldn’t be able to concentrate. We’re going to have a teleprompter on that day. So don’t worry about it.”

So Moore worked on it normally, she said, “like I worked on everything else in the movie. So when we got to it, I knew it. I didn’t need a teleprompter. He knew instinctively as a director and an actor that what scares us sometimes is just a volume of language. He didn’t want to freeze me up. And having a partner like Paul who was so awake and aware and generous made it a pleasure. We were enjoying it when we did shoot it.”

Moore and Giamatti had never worked together before. She once introduced herself to him in a bookstore in Montauk. “He was very shy,” she said. “He is the greatest scene partner. I didn’t expect him to be so generous. He’s so funny, and he’s so dear. He’s present, incredibly modest, and as a partner, so available. Paul and I would work on it occasionally. When we were doing that scene, the rhythm was so important in it. You throw something, he hits it right back. It was our sense together of keeping it aloft, keeping it moving, keeping the river flowing. It felt electric with the two of us.”

The big blowout happens early in the story. “In a lot of movies, that kind of set piece would happen later,” said Moore. “Instead, it’s like a discovery place. It’s where she starts to begin to unlock herself emotionally, but she doesn’t learn from it. She comes in the next day, and starts to rehearse. And her belief is that acting is size, that it’s just huge, right? That’s when she starts yelling. She thinks it’s about being loud, which then allows her to go on the next journey with Jerry, where he says, ‘Let’s talk about feeling and reality and intention.’ So she’s slowly putting these pieces together. But that’s the first moment where she attaches something outside of herself to her own emotion.”

The whole shoot was fast, as Eisenberg didn’t have time to muck about and often shot just one take of a scene. “She and Paul Giamatti are so good on take one,” said Eisenberg. “It’s embarrassing. This is a small budget movie. The first two days of our schedule, we filmed in one day. The first two days, which were big ensemble musical numbers, we filmed in one day because we were prepared as a crew, but the actors were perfect on take one.”

Moore didn’t feel rushed. “It doesn’t feel, working with Jesse, like you’re moving too fast,” she said. “Working in independent film, you’re always moving quickly because you need to. You don’t have the time. You don’t have the money. So you want to move through things quickly. But I never felt rushed with him. I never I never felt like I was leaving something, that I didn’t get to complete something.”

The challenge for Moore, as it is for every actor shooting out of order, was making her character changes seamless. Eisenberg started with the theater scenes, then shot her family, and then jumped into Mona’s increasing weirdness. “The hardest thing always is making sure that you’ve pitched things correctly,” Moore said. “You want to make sure that you’ve managed to match it to another scene. So it was always hard to figure out. That’s our job.”

Eisenberg wanted Mona to move from looking quite childlike in the beginning, and swiftly move through her evolving transformations. Moore had fun with the costumes, figuring out the crazy wigs, makeup, and outfits in the second half. “Jesse had written that Mona electrocutes herself and destroys her hair, and that she was going to get her hair cut,” said Moore, “but he hadn’t written in a color change. We were messing around with it and trying to figure out what to do with hair and makeup and wardrobe and we had this idea that by having her dye her hair dark and chop it off, I wanted to homage the great ladies of musical theater, Liza Minnelli and Chita Rivera and Patti LuPone. It’s a wonderful Easter egg for that character.”

Making everything easier for Moore was actor-turned-director Eisenberg, who’d tell her when to ‘raise the stakes’ or ‘go hotter.’ “He’s maybe the most collaborative person I’ve ever worked with my entire life,” said Moore. “He listens to everyone. He asks people for opinions. He’ll ask people for notes, in a way that I would be like, ‘you don’t have to do that. This is your movie. It’s your creation.’ But he does collate opinion in a way. He’s fascinating in his generosity.”

Needless to say, singing her centerpiece song (“This City May Have Chewed Me Up (But It Hasn’t Spit Me Out”) was nervous-making, given that Moore was surrounded by Broadway super-belters like Tony winners Danny Burstein and Bonnie Tillman. “These people have the voices of angels,” said Moore. “When I did sing that song for the first time, and they’re all sitting there watching me, I think they did feel worried for me because they have so much ease. The song that she sings is so beautiful. In the singing of the song, she’s attaching her own emotional experience suddenly to the song. She understands the song in the moment she’s singing that. Somehow she wants more, and she knows that this is an avenue for her to find that. And so it’s a journey back to herself: finding that creativity and connection and community brings her to an essential sense of self.”

If degree of difficulty counts with Oscar voters, Moore may have that advantage.

entry.title: Our Plea to the New DC Studios Head: No More Shared Universe!
entry.summary: With James Gunn and Peter Safran out at DC Studios, their replacement should not try and map out an ambitious, 10-year, connected universe of films.
entry.content:
The DCU is dead before it even started.

Four years ago, DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran relaunched the comics brand with grand ambitions to build a Marvel Cinematic Universe of their own with a crop of characters they believed to be superior to what Marvel and Disney had. They controlled Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Green Lantern, The Flash, and a whole bunch more they could mold as they saw fit, and they promised they would fix the flawed Marvel Studios system of greenlighting projects before a strong screenplay was in place. They announced a massive slate of 10 films and series right out of the gate and had other expectations that stars they cast today would appear in future DC films for the long haul. Above all, they were going to be careful with the brand.

Related Stories
DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn, Peter Safran Stepping Down as Co-CEOs, Marvel Vet Jeremy Latcham Named Chief Creative Officer
James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next

“No one was minding the mint,” Gunn said back in January 2023 in a telling quote. “They were just giving away IP like they were party favors to any creators who smiled at them. What we are going to do is promise that everything from our first project going forward is going to be unified.”

The real world quickly caught up to Gunn and Safran. In a move beyond their control, ownership of DC Studios changed hands yet again from Warner Bros. Discovery to Skydance, and now just four years, three films, and a couple of TV shows into their tenure, they’re out. Taking the reins is Jeremy Latcham, not a household name the way Kevin Feige or some of his lieutenants have been, but an architect of the early stages of the MCU and a key, former executive at Marvel (he left for an independent label of his own in 2017). He has comic book chops, having produced “The Avengers,” the first MCU “Spider-Man,” and more.

Because the ball didn’t really get rolling at DC Studios in the short time Gunn and Safran were on board, and because Latcham still has a lingering slate that includes a second “Superman” movie that’s already in the can and a second “The Batman” movie in the works that isn’t even connected to the DCU anyway, as he begins to map out his own ambitions for the next era of DC movies and series, we have a simple plea: no more shared universes. Please. We beg you. Enough already.

Do not try and build the next MCU or even the next DC(E)U or whatever you want to call it. Just make some really good superhero movies with the characters and brands people love.

Books have been and will be written about the producing success story Kevin Feige managed with the MCU, and David Ellison, fanboy that he is, would surely love to have his own version of “The Avengers.” Who wouldn’t? We’ve seen other studios try and recreate the MCU formula with their own IP, like the Godzilla vs. Kong-iverse from WB and Legendary or the incredibly misguided plan for a Universal monster-verse that fizzled out with Tom Cruise’s “The Mummy.“

Truth be told, Marvel is trying to reconstruct its own formula ever since “Avengers: Endgame,” and it has been a mixed bag. Sure, there were a few billion-dollar hits in there like “Deadpool & Wolverine” and this year’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” and “Avengers: Doomsday” too figures to be huge, but other new characters and would-be franchises like “Eternals” or “Shang-Chi” have gone through fits and stops. Movies like a “Blade” reboot have never been able to get off the ground as Marvel tries to fit a square peg into a round hole. Marvel has been forced to recast and scramble its carefully laid plans amid the controversy around Jonathan Majors. And the sheer glut of TV shows over the last few years has created immense homework for people that has led the actual flagship movies to drop off precipitously at the box office.

Is that what DC Studios really wants? More of that drama and headache? It feels like we’re well beyond the era where audiences are willing to commit for every new episode of a yearslong cinematic saga. Surely whatever vision Gunn and Safran had was grand, especially if you’re a real fan of those characters and want to see them all come together as the Justice League yet again, but it doesn’t feel like today’s young audiences want to sign up for that.

Gunn and Safran actually immediately ran into this problem as they tried to bridge the gap between the old DCEU and the new DCU they were building. People knew “The Flash” and “Aquaman 2” weren’t going to be part of the future, even as Gunn and Safran paid lip service to the idea and played coy about having some of these actors reprising their roles in the new universe. (Remember when Henry Cavill thought for a minute he was playing Superman again?) The films underwhelmed at the box office as a result, and it created confusion among casual fans as the execs were forced to dance around the fanboys and the Snyder Army.

Audiences, though, have demonstrated that superhero movies still matter when they feature characters they care about. “Spider-Man” stayed away for about five years, and “Brand New Day” is now one of the highest-grossing movies of all time. We hadn’t had a proper, standalone “Superman” movie in years, and it proved to be a great launching pad for Gunn’s slate, earning $618.7 million worldwide. There’s still huge excitement for “The Batman: Part II” from Matt Reeves, and there’s never been any pretense that it’s connected to some more important lore or that Pattinson’s Bruce Wayne might show up in a theoretical “Wonder Woman” sequel a decade down the road. People just really like Batman.

So what do you do now if you’re Latcham and have to answer to Ellison and former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz? It would make sense to just demonstrate how you’re going to make the most of the IP that you have. Signaling to audiences (and shareholders) that your next Wonder Woman movie won’t come out until 2037 because you’re mapping out the shared universe for how to carefully introduce all these characters doesn’t sound like the best approach. Just hire smart writers, entrust visionary directors, and make some good movies. It worked with “The Batman.”

This, of course, does not mean don’t make your big “Justice League” team up movie or don’t build a new franchise out of “Teen Titans.” It just means that times and appetites have changed from the pre-Covid and even pre-streaming boom MCU era when “Guardians of the Galaxy” could be a hit (in part) because of how it teased the arrival of Thanos and the Infinity Stones. Audiences have become more discerning about what they define as an event film, and DC Studios can beat Marvel at its own game so long as DC stops trying to become Marvel.

Start by being the best version of DC.

entry.title: Rejected Twice by Sundance, ‘Mouse’ Is One of the Year’s Best Movies. Why Aren’t More People Talking About It?
entry.summary: Alex Thompson and Kelly O'Sullivan talk the journey to 'Mouse,' which Sundance rejected twice.
entry.content:
Don’t be surprised if you emerge from Alex Thompson and Kelly O’Sullivan’s piercingly moving coming-of-age grief dramedy “Mouse” in a puddle of tears. Graceful in technique, compassionate in its writing, this movie, one of the year’s best, is a crying machine. But that’s not to say this story of a high school girl’s (Katherine Mallen Kupferer, astonishing) formative first encounter with major loss is any bit manipulative.

As heartbreak ripples through a small town, “Mouse” has the texture and deep feeling of Kenneth Lonergan’s post-9/11 New York City drama “Margaret,” starring Anna Paquin as a precocious teenager in freefall after witnessing a pedestrian’s brutal death. Unlike “Margaret,” “Mouse” didn’t take over half a decade to reach screens after production wrapped, but the road was still paved with rejection (baffling in retrospect) for Chicago directing duo Thompson and O’Sullivan.

Related Stories
From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race
How John Malkovich Nailed the Role of His Career with ‘Wild Horse Nine’

With “Mouse,” the filmmakers found themselves at the Berlin Film Festival for the first time back in February — even as an American indie set in Arkansas about the challenges of coming of age feels like catnip for a festival like Sundance, where such topics are historically de rigueur. And Thompson and O’Sullivan had been to Sundance before, with their critically championed 2024 comedy-drama “Ghostlight,” about an emotionally ramshackle, rookie community theater production of “Romeo and Juliet.” While placement at the legacy indie festival, headed to Boulder in January, doesn’t always mean you’re grandfathered into the acceptance pipeline for your next movie, it was still a surprise to the directors (who are also life partners with two children) when Sundance turned down “Mouse” not once, but twice.

“To be totally fair, we submitted before we probably should have, with a long cut,” O’Sullivan told IndieWire over Zoom. “Apparently, it didn’t matter,” Thompson added.

“We submitted it again the next year, when it was tighter,” added O’Sullivan, though the filmmakers were dismissed again. “The feedback that we got — and again, this is a game of telephone, so we don’t know — is that it had real champions, but that it also had people who didn’t get it. Yes, it was crushing. It was confusing. More than anything, I was like, ‘Wait, but people did such great work on this movie. The work is incredible.’ And not ours even, but Sophie [Okonedo] and Katherine [Mallen Kupferer], and the crew, I was like, ‘I feel like they deserve a really big stage.’”

Luckily, the Berlin Film Festival stepped in to program “Mouse” in the Panorama section, marking Thompson and O’Sullivan’s first bow at a European fest, where it grabbed strong reviews. And, as the filmmakers point out, that festival turned out to be the proper home. (Berlin, after all, just had its strongest lineup in years, under artistic director Tricia Tuttle’s second festival.)

“It really was hard for a moment, and then we heard back from Berlin, and it kind of felt like a career opportunity that went way beyond Sundance,” Thompson said. “Tapping into the narrative outside of the American indie felt like something we’d always aspired to. And those are the films that I identify with the most, the sort of work that comes out of those great European festivals. The most jealous and childish I am is every year when the Venice reviews start coming out, and it’s like, ‘Ah, well, those all sound great.’ And Cannes and Berlin, and our favorite festivals, we have a relationship with Thessaloniki and American Film Festival in Wrocław, and to have that stage at Berlin, it’s like this sort of historic stage. It’s absolutely mind-blowing. I’ve never been in a theater that big with a movie.”

A Gotham nominee for Best Feature, “Mouse” is now quietly in theaters from Independent Film Company. (A sparsely attended Academy screening also took place in Los Angeles over the weekend.) Film chatterers may deem this a “small” movie in a year of “You Can See Everything” and “La Bola Negra,” it is huge in every way.

The film follows Minnie Dunn (Kupferer), who, just as she’s about to enter her senior year, is dealt a life-altering loss. It’s 2002, Michelle Branch is on the radio, and September 11 is not even a year out of view. Faced with a hole in her life in the shape of her lifelong best friend after a tragic accident, Minnie forms a tight bond with the girl’s British stay-at-home mother, Helen (Sophie Okonedo, luminescent here), mourning on her own. Meanwhile, Minnie’s classmates all but literally compete to see who can grieve the loudest in the form of a talent show. “Mouse” is about the centrifugal force of grief and how life goes on around you, but you’re still stuck in the same place.

Big on emotional generosity and ace turns from the filmmakers’ stable of theater-based Chicago actors — including Kupferer and her real-life mother Tara Mallen, who plays Minnie’s struggling, lower-middle-class mom onscreen — “Mouse” deserves as much attention as any of the year’s best films. The grand ambition of “Mouse” and its emotional dividends and wonderful performances suggest it could’ve cleaned up at Telluride or even Toronto, where, in the latter case, a number of indie films flopped, and even the most acclaimed are still searching for distribution.

“Rejected, rejected,” O’Sullivan laughed, later adding, “We understand how complicated programming a festival is, and we don’t feel entitled to be programmed anywhere. We’re grateful to every festival that’s given us a slot.”

She wrote the script for “Mouse” in 2019, around the time their debut feature as collaborators, “Saint Frances,” opened at SXSW. That microbudget indie, directed by Thompson and starring O’Sullivan as a drifting 34-year-old nanny in Chicago, won the Austin festival’s audience award and later earned a John Cassavetes Spirit Award nomination. “Mouse” was actually meant to be their next feature, with one financier, a cushier budget, and a slightly different cast — until the strikes changed their plans, leading to “Ghostlight” as their Sundance debut on a smaller scale.

Based on O’Sullivan’s own experience with loss as a teen, “Mouse” picked back up in fall 2024, shooting on location in her home state of Arkansas. “We were amazingly able to retain the vision” of “Mouse” from before the strikes, she said. “Nothing got cut for budget.”

Thompson, who produced the film, said, “Knowing the budget so intimately, I guess that’s my superpower on the producing side that most directors don’t have is I just get really intimate with the budget. And it seems really boring, but it’s kind of like a script where if you don’t have the means, if it’s not there in the budget, it’s not going to happen… A lot of directors I talked to have been like, ‘Oh, well, my producer said we couldn’t do a rain tower, or my producers said we couldn’t do this shot because we can’t afford it.’ And it’s like, well, you can pretty much afford anything. You just have to give somewhere else. We tend to make really ambitious one-liners like schedules. We had 30 days on this, but that ended up being a two-hour and 15-minute movie, and we cut 20 minutes.”

When asked about the “Mouse” budget, he said, “I think we can say. We’re already underdogs. We might as well say. It was $3 million.”

And it’s $3 million, well-budgeted and in true indie spirit — like a scene where Minnie and her friends watch “Titanic” in a parent’s basement during one of those classic sleepovers where private confidences spill out, insulated from the adult world upstairs and outside.

“We didn’t even try to get the rights to ‘Titanic,’ but we’re mixing at Skywalker,” Thompson said. “They have the entire effects library for ‘Titanic’ … so we rebuilt the dance scene in ‘Titanic’ and used public-domain Irish music, and then Kelly and [producer] Pierce Cravens do the voices of Leo and Kate off in a room being like, ‘I feel so young,’ or something, whatever that is. If you watch the movie, you think they’re watching ‘Titanic’ in the basement, but it’s a totally constructed thing because we’re like, ‘We can’t get the rights to this.'”

On top of “Mouse” already dwelling on a very specific point of loss from O’Sullivan’s own childhood, the filmmaker’s mother also died in Arkansas toward the end of production. That meant she was actively grieving while also leading a set, alongside her partner.

“It was so bizarre,” O’Sullivan said. “She died when we had a week and a half left to shoot… It was incredibly complicated. I just couldn’t believe the timing of it for so many different reasons. I mean, one of which is just that it took forever to make this movie, but the movie allowed me to be there literally when she died. I didn’t have to get on a plane. But then when I was back on set, I just kept hearing these lines that I had written, and they took on a whole new meaning… lines that I had sort of written in a very theoretical way all of a sudden were hitting me in a, ‘God, I can’t believe how true this was, and I didn’t even know.'”

The autobiography that drove “Mouse” extended behind the scenes in even more literal ways. Christen Pitts, the choreographer behind the movie’s climactic ballet elegy sequence set to a cover of Cyndi Lauper’s “Time After Time,” was O’Sullivan’s high school dance teacher. “It feels like so many different chapters of my life are just compressing into the same space, and it feels like a culmination of my entire adult life and teenage years and echoes of the past existing,” O’Sullivan said.

Thompson and O’Sullivan have maintained their filmmaking footprint in and around Chicago — even as “Mouse” brought them to Arkansas — and they don’t feel especially tempted to make the leap to Hollywood, though there have been offers.

“I just write from a place of experience most of the time, and I don’t know, I’ve seen so many movies set in L.A. and New York, and I actually don’t identify with those towns,” O’Sullivan said. “I feel like enough people are doing that, and I like writing from a place of specificity … I’ve spent maybe a year in both places cumulatively. It doesn’t feel like a character that I personally need to explore. But having said that, if I spent more time there, it felt like a story was necessarily set there. I’d be open to it. I just don’t feel compelled to.”

“We really want to have a body of work,” Thompson said. “The people I admire the most are Steven Soderbergh and Sidney Lumet, directors who have dozens of films by the time they stop, and Soderbergh has not stopped, obviously.” He doesn’t know that a move to Los Angeles is possible given their artistic goals. “We’ve gone out on meetings, we’ve done pitches, we’ve considered projects from studios, and the timeline always felt kind of like it just hasn’t really worked out. ‘Mouse’ was so close to being that thing, and then the writers’ strike, and the SAG strike, we lost a cast member, and it just all fell away. So we just thought, ‘What if we just do what we did on ‘Ghostlight,’ but on steroids? If I can raise half a million dollars, I wonder if we can raise three.”

With the filmmakers now set up at Gersh talent agency, he added, “If we want to make a movie every 15 months, we probably can’t do that in the studio system. I think we both like the idea of playing in a bigger sandbox and taking the intimacy, taking all the things we’ve learned, and working in a bigger sandbox. I don’t think that’s unattractive, but it’s just, for the way we work, this has made the most sense so far.”

Next up, Thompson directed a high-concept body-swap comedy starring the “Ghostlight” father-daughter (and real-life father-daughter) team of “Mouse” star Katherine Mallen Kupferer with Keith Kupferer. Plus, they’ve co-directed “The Steel Harp,” starring Lois Smith and O’Sullivan in a return to acting. Both are expected in 2027.

“We shoot on the same lenses as ‘Saint Frances,’ same aspect ratio as ‘Mouse,’ in a world that winks at a bigger sandbox,” Thompson said of the body swap movie. “It’s a total gamble. I’ve got no idea if it’s going to work… It seems to be quite funny according to my three-year-old.”

“Mouse” is now playing in New York and Los Angeles, with a wider expansion to follow in November.

entry.title: DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn, Peter Safran Stepping Down as Co-CEOs, Marvel Vet Jeremy Latcham Named Chief Creative Officer
entry.summary: In a shakeup at DC Studios, James Gunn, Peter Safran will step down as co-heads while Jeremy Latcham has been named president.
entry.content:
James Gunn and Peter Safran are out as heads of DC Studios.

The move comes after Skydance closed its $110 billion deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery in October. Jeremy Latcham, who helped shape the Marvel Cinematic Universe, has been appointed president and chief creative officer, DC Studios, beginning December 1, 2026.

Gunn and Safran joined the company four years ago with the goal of making DC a true challenger to the MCU, but they’ve had mixed success. “Superman,” which Gunn directed, was a hit at the box office, but “Supergirl” bombed and “Clayface,” an R-rated body horror film, has performed modestly. The pair also launched new series based on the comic book company’s characters, including “Peacemaker” and “Lanterns.” Gunn has one more film on the horizon, the “Superman” sequel, “Man of Tomorrow,” which opens next year.

Related Stories
James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Experiment: What’s Working, What Isn’t, and What’s Next
‘Clayface’ Tops the Box Office with $24 Million. What Does It Signal About DC Studios’ Latest Reboot?

“James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we’re incredibly proud of,” David Ellison, Chairman and CEO, and Ynon Kreiz, Co-CEO, of Skydance said in a statement. “We’re grateful for their passion, contributions, and commitment to this legendary brand. Jeremy has been a longtime creative partner to both, and we have complete confidence that James and Peter will ensure a smooth, collaborative transition and continue this work with care. We look forward to working with Jeremy to build the next generation of DC storytelling and to doubling down on our commitment to fans.”

In a separate statement, Gunn and Safran said, “Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore ‘Superman’ to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with ‘Peacemaker,’ ‘Creature Commandos,’ ‘Lanterns,’ and ‘Clayface.’ We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews, and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter.”

Latcham will lead DC’s film, television, and animation slate. He will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, Co-Chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group.

“Jeremy brings a deep reverence for DC and its passionate fanbase, recognizing that they are the very foundation of this storied, multigenerational brand,” said Goldberg and Greenstein. “Under his leadership, every film and television show will be ushered from start to finish through the prism of the legions of fans who love and champion it. Jeremy’s track record exemplifies the excellence he will bring to building out DC and the many beloved characters within it.”

At Marvel, Latcham produced several of the company’s biggest hits, including “The Avengers,” “Spider-Man: Homecoming,” “Iron Man 2,” and “Guardians of the Galaxy,” which Gunn directed. As an independent producer, his credits include “Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves” and “The Breadwinner.”

Latcham faces a steep challenge. DC has suffered from a lack of consistency in its creative direction. The studio was initially overseen by comic book veterans Geoff Johns and Jon Berg, who were later replaced by veteran producer Walter Hamada, before he too was ousted. Over that time, DC had hits such as “Aquaman” and “Wonder Woman,” but they were outweighed by costly failures like “Justice League” and “The Flash.”

When Discovery bought Warner Bros. in 2022, David Zaslav personally courted Gunn and Safran to turn the ship around. But the timing was tricky. Comic book movies remain popular, at least the ones featuring marquee heroes like Spider-Man or Batman, but audiences have grown more discerning. They are less likely to show up for second- or third-tier characters (see: Supergirl). So it will fall to Latcham to figure out a new strategy to meet the moment, one that either builds on Gunn and Safran’s foundation or takes the studio in yet another direction.

entry.title: From Los Javis to Lord and Miller, Director Duos Are a High-Risk, High-Reward Prospect in the Oscar Race
entry.summary: Awards bodies often overlook director duos, but pairs like Los Javis and Lord and Miller could make Best Director Oscar history with their 2026 films.
entry.content:
From “Project Hail Mary” to “La Bola Negra” and “You Can See Everything,” this awards season is dominated by director duos.

Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, better known as Los Javis, are seen as locks for “La Bola Negra,” the Netflix-backed gay historical epic, while longtime collaborators Phil Lord and Chris Miller are also firmly in the Oscar conversation for their work on “Project Hail Mary.” Then there’s Emmy nominee Nathan Fielder teaming up with documentary-world wunderkind Lance Oppenheim on “You Can See Everything,” a less conventional contender, but one that could muscle itself into the race thanks to its box office success.

Related Stories
How John Malkovich Nailed the Role of His Career with ‘Wild Horse Nine’
‘Half Nelson’ at 20: How a $700,000 Indie Addiction Drama Earned Ryan Gosling His First Oscar Nod

Expand the scope further, and there’s recent indie box office success “Wicker” from husband-and-wife filmmaking duo Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson. Plus “Clarissa” from brothers Arie and Chuko Esiri, and “Mouse” from director couple Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson, which picked up a Gotham Best Feature nom.

That’s six different films in this year’s awards conversation, suggesting director duos are becoming more common in filmmaking overall. But in terms of Oscar recognition, only five films across the Academy Awards‘ 98-year history have had their filmmaker duos nominated for Best Director. More than one team nominated for Best Director this season would be a record.

So what makes director duos so rare at the Oscars? Much of it comes down to the Directors Guild of America. Keep in mind, Best Director nominations are determined by the contenders’ peers in the Directors Branch, so even though the DGA is a separate group with its own eligibility rules for the DGA Awards, the guild overlaps enough with the Academy to set the tone. The DGA also has a bylaw that states, “One Director to a Film.” The logic behind the rule, established in 1978, is to prevent anyone, especially producers, from delegating tasks to other members of a director’s team. Director duos can request a waiver, but they must prove they intend to be lifelong collaborators.

The “One Director to a Film” mentality is another major hurdle for “You Can See Everything” directors Fielder and Oppenheim in particular, as both filmmakers had established solo careers before teaming up. Meanwhile, the rest of the class of 2026 director duos have been collaborators from the start of their careers, with Los Javis and Lord and Miller, the two most viable Best Director candidates, even having shorthand nicknames within the industry. “You Can See Everything” has already been deemed ineligible for a Best Director nomination at the DGA Awards, because the category does not include documentaries.

Despite the hurdles they must overcome, director duos often go on to win Oscars if they secure a nomination. That was the case for “West Side Story” directors Robert Wise and Jerome Robbins in 1962, for “No Country for Old Men” directors Joel and Ethan Coen in 2008, and most recently for “Everything Everywhere All at Once” directors Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert (aka Daniels) in 2023.

Of the two director duos that fell short, one was the Coen Brothers again for “True Grit” in 2011, only three years after they won the Best Director Oscar. That makes “Heaven Can Wait” helmers Warren Beatty and Buck Henry the only director duo that didn’t win the Oscar the first time they were nominated as a pair. Henry and Beatty would never direct together again, and Beatty would win the Oscar for directing “Reds” three years after “Heaven Can Wait” came out in 1978.

So while there’s a tremendous barrier for entry, if any of the director duos in the awards mix this year are able to secure a Best Director nomination, history indicates they should probably have an acceptance speech ready.

entry.title: How John Malkovich Nailed the Role of His Career with ‘Wild Horse Nine’
entry.summary: John Malkovich on nailing his role as a CIA troublemaker in 'Wild Horse Nine,' a part that could get him an Oscar.
entry.content:
Editor’s Note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Telluride Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures opened “Wild Horse Nine” in select theaters on November 6.

While early “Wild Horse Nine” press screenings in Los Angeles and New York got the ball rolling, the first whiff of a strong public reaction was the Venice Film Festival, where edgy auteur Martin McDonagh, John Malkovich, and Sam Rockwell soaked up sustained applause. Then they were whisked to the Colorado Rockies to screen the movie in Telluride.

Instantly, Malkovich jumped up the Best Actor rankings for what would be his third Oscar nomination. His first two were for Supporting Actor, in 1985 for “Places in the Heart,” and 1993 for “In the Line of Fire.” Now the movie is screening at the Toronto International Film Festival ahead of its November 6 release.

Related Stories
‘Half Nelson’ at 20: How a $700,000 Indie Addiction Drama Earned Ryan Gosling His First Oscar Nod
Cinematographers’ Favorite Festival Is All About AI This Year — but Artists Still Hate the Tech

I caught up with Malkovich in the back of a large black SUV parked in front of the Herzog Theatre before his first of two Telluride Tributes.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

Anne Thompson: How did you first get to know Martin McDonagh?

John Malkovich: I was offered a couple things of Martin’s over the years. One, “Seven Psychopaths,” one, [the play] “A Behanding in Spokane,” but I couldn’t do it. I was busy. I love the scripts, but I couldn’t do it, and so then this came. I thought the thing was great. Beautiful piece of writing, just a perfect screenplay, and I couldn’t believe I got sent it. I couldn’t believe he asked me to do it.

It’s a juicy lead.

Yeah. So I said, “Yeah!” with no hesitation at all. I have two little granddaughters. I don’t love being away for two, three months, whatever. But it’s part of the job, so you got to do it. We met in London because I’d never met Martin. We rehearsed five to six days in London with Sam, who I love. I’d worked with him before on “The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy,” not a long gig, but I knew Sam a bit socially. And I’d worked with Buscemi before twice because he was in our film “Ghost World,” and we worked together in “Con Air.” Sam and I hit it off, workwise, very well, very quickly.

You may not agree, but I think Sam receded slightly and supported you in an amazing way. I find it moving, actually, that he did this for you. Do you feel that’s what he did?

Yes and no. I think he played his part. And the part [of Lee] is slightly recessive in that sense. Chris is the older one. He’s the wild card. He’s killed whatever, 168 people, but apparently none while they were eating. And he’s a legend in the CIA. Sam is an exceptionally generous actor, as generous as you could ever find, you couldn’t ask for a better partner in every way.

You’ve been doing this a long time. Your first Oscar nomination was in 1985. That’s over 40 years ago. Both your nominations have been for Supporting Actor. Are you a character actor?

I’ve had leading roles. But people don’t understand what a role is, the general public or anybody except actors. First of all, you can be a terrific actor in anything, but if the film isn’t good, it’s utterly meaningless. You may as well not have bothered. You may as well not have done it. It’s a waste of time. For a good role to be really good, people have to not just like the way you do that, but like what the character is doing, and understand it if they don’t like it, and they have to like the arc of the character. The best performances I gave would have been on stage first of all, but secondly, those in the cinema wouldn’t necessarily be in good movies, ugh. And that, on a certain level, has precious little to do with performance X, Y, Z. That’s just one small part of a movie.

In this case, you’re given an extraordinary amount of verbiage. So you had to make the rhythm of it, the sense of it, the emotion of it. Sometimes it’s hilariously funny, sometimes sad, and you run that gamut.

Yeah, but that’s great writing. This material, I believe, causes a big wave, and you ride that wave where it’s going, through comedy, through drama, through tragedy, even if that’s the nature of a particular text, and that’s what actors do. The collision between the public and the material is caused by a recognition in their lives.

Our CIA agent Chris is messing around with Chile in 1973 as Pinochet waits in the wings.

November 22, 1963 is a trauma, as is September 11, 2001, and 1973 in Chile. For those of us who were alive at that time, it’s immutable. Doesn’t matter your politics then or now, or if you had any. Doesn’t matter anything. I directed Don DeLillo’s great novel “Libra,” adapted it for the stage with Don, and Don referred to it in the book as the seven seconds that broke the back of the American century in Chile and it was not the only place on earth: Chile, Argentina, Brazil, Peru, Ecuador.

We were bad.

And various actors have been bad along with us, and possibly not worse, but the birthday party was spoiled. What’s left, and it caused generations of pain, of nihilism, of loss of innocence, of loss of faith in a political system. People everywhere can understand that, and Martin mines that beautifully. It’s beautifully structured in the writing and modulated in the filmmaking. So the wave is there.

Your character is fun to watch because he’s unfettered, he’s unleashed, he doesn’t give a fuck anymore. He’s just going to say what he wants to say, and he’s going to tell the truth.

And people appreciate that because in this culture, it’s very odd. You say this word or that word, and the anti-social media mob goes berserk. I don’t have social media. I don’t want it designated to me in the slightest. I don’t care what they say. They can say whatever they want, and so can people who offend you. They can say whatever they want, and voila, who cares? And this idea that you can’t say that because it’s offensive to this or that, and covers everything and every topic and every subject and every blah blah blah seems incredibly dumb. It’s a dumb world.

Well, that’s one of the great things about being a certain age, right? You don’t care anymore. He doesn’t, and maybe you don’t.

I stay off [social media] because I don’t see the value. I’m doing things. If people like them, beautiful. If they hate them, beautiful. I do a [stage and short film] piece called “The Music Critic,” which is all the worst reviews of all the most beautiful pieces of classical music in the world. They were all trashed. They were all hated. So what? Get used to it. Grow a thick skin, go on with your life, do what you think is good.

That’s good advice for everyone.

entry.title: ‘Half Nelson’ at 20: How a $700,000 Indie Addiction Drama Earned Ryan Gosling His First Oscar Nod
entry.summary: Filmmakers Ryan Fleck and Anna Boden look back on 'Half Nelson' at 20. The film earned Ryan Gosling his first Oscar nomination.
entry.content:
“He said it felt like we were the kind of people who talked about the script like we were plotting to build a bomb,” laughed Ryan Fleck, remembering how he and his longtime filmmaker partner, Anna Boden, convinced Ryan Gosling to star in their feature debut, “Half Nelson.” “It was probably a little bit true though,” adds Boden. “We hadn’t done much except try to make this movie for a long time, and maybe that came off the page. Maybe he was like, ‘Let’s just throw them a bone!’”

It was the right choice. “Half Nelson” arrived in 2006, an era when introspective indies still had time to flourish theatrically and find their crowd — and that’s exactly what happened. Filmed for just $700,000, Fleck and Boden’s first film turned a limited theatrical run into a $4.9 million global box office haul, while earning their leading man his first Best Actor Oscar nod. Looking back, it’s undoubtedly a success story — but far from a predictable one.

Related Stories
Cinematographers’ Favorite Festival Is All About AI This Year — but Artists Still Hate the Tech
‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards

“The thing about not yet being a professional filmmaker is you’ve got time until someone greenlights your movie, so there was lots of time,” said Fleck, recalling the movie’s long road to production. The pair met on a summer filmmaking course at NYU in the early aughts and quickly realized they wanted to work together. “We were always big movie fans, and the ones that moved me the most were films like ‘Midnight Cowboy’ and ‘Harold and Maude.’ They all had flawed people at their core. We started there and began digging into things we knew a little about.”

Together, they spliced their own flawed character with themes of isolation and addiction, and before long they had someone they felt they could form a feature around. Their idea centered on Dan Dunne (Gosling), a twenty-something middle-school teacher and struggling creative balancing full-time work with a freebasing addiction, and Drey (Shareeka Epps), the young student who stumbles on his secret. That was their starting point, but over time, it evolved.

“When we first started writing in 2002 or 2003, it felt like a lot of young people had all this energy but didn’t know how to affect change in the world around them,” said Boden, explaining how external conflicts like America’s involvement with the Afghanistan war impacted the story they wanted to tell. “We were finding this character that was going through that too, in his own way.”

Fleck unpacked this disconnect further: “[Dan] understands how history, politics and change work outside of himself but he can’t quite get it under control within himself.”

Despite having a finished screenplay, securing a green light proved elusive. However, instead of feeling dejected, the pair got to work. “We had this script but literally didn’t have anybody to give it to, so we made a short because that was something we did know how to do. We focused on the young student character, changing her from male to female and casting somebody from a local middle school,” said Boden, of Epps’ entry into the project. In fact, all the actors in their short “Gowanus, Brooklyn” were nonprofessionals. “It was a great way of working through the ideas, emotions and feelings we were trying to get across. Going back to the script after that deepened it a lot.”

Being proactive paid off. After a successful Sundance screening, “Gowanus, Brooklyn” bagged 2004’s Grand Jury Prize, paving the way for the feature they’d initially dreamed of — or so they thought. “I remember coming off stage and whispering to Anna, ‘I think this means we’re going to get to make our feature,’” said Fleck, laughing at his naivety. “It didn’t make it easy, but it certainly made it a more clear path.”

The win secured the duo an agent and key industry connections, through which their feature script reached their would-be leading man. Looking back, it’s easy to see someone as multi-faceted as Gosling deliver on the many faces this role required. Dan’s someone who’s simultaneously dejected, drug-addled and lost — but also inspirational, trusted and boasting a strong moral compass. Easy for someone with Gosling’s skillset, right? Fleck and Boden weren’t convinced right away.

“It had been written for someone a little bit older than him,” revealed Boden, describing the struggle of seeing the world-weary Dan in 24-year-old Gosling. “I remember when he met us, he’d grown his chin hairs out and looked a little older.” Fleck has similar memories: “It wasn’t immediate. We thought of somebody who had more life experience. He didn’t have the body of work he has now, but he just had this old-soul quality to him. He didn’t seem 24.”

Gosling threw himself into the role. “We introduced him to a public school teacher who was about his age so he could shadow him,” explained Boden. “Ryan picked up all these subtle little things from him, like wearing rubber bands around his wrists. The guy ended up looking so much like him that we cast him as Dan’s brother.” His ability to keep things loose lent itself to the pair’s fly-on-the-wall style, too. “Some of those classroom scenes have a very spontaneous feel,” she added, confirming that the students often didn’t know what Gosling was going to ask. “Some of their lines were scripted, some weren’t. They were reacting in real-time.”

Then there was the heavy stuff, like Drey unceremoniously discovering Dan’s freebasing habit in the school bathroom. As an inner-city teen, she’s caught in her own internal battle between a life of honest education and the quick wins of neighborhood crime, tempted by toxic family friend Frank (Anthony Mackie). It’s a challenging role for any actor, let alone someone making their feature debut.

“The other big thing [Ryan] brought was stripping away the dialogue. The scene where Drey is taking care of him after his overdose felt so much more visceral without any lines. You could hear a pin drop,” said Boden.

“I think Shareeka was genuinely frightened,” recalled Fleck. “There’s such an intensity… I think she was genuinely concerned for him — and I was concerned for her watching it. I was just blown away, like ‘Wow. These people are really good.’”

Meanwhile, low-level dealer Frank offers Drey his own guidance in a morally blurry role that’s part friend, part corruptor. “[Anthony] immediately got what we were going for,” said Boden. “Frank isn’t a cartel guy or a big kingpin. He’s your working-class drug dealer making just enough to live on. It’s something that should feel relatable, even though he’s doing something illegal. Anthony and Shareeka immediately clicked. You can feel it on screen.”

To score their first film, the duo drew inspiration from one of their favorites, Hal Ashby’s “Harold and Maude,” a film that dedicates its entire soundtrack to one artist: Cat Stevens. For “Half Nelson,” Fleck and Boden chose Canadian indie-rock collective Broken Social Scene, blending their stark imagery with a dreamy sound that delivered a deftly emotional punch.

“A friend of Anna’s introduced us to their music, and we became obsessed,” said Fleck, explaining the choice. “When you put their music against some of the images we were playing with, it gave us goosebumps.”

There was just one issue: They needed the band’s permission. Luckily, they had a connection to Broken Social Scene lead singer Kevin Drew — but the Canadian musician was a bit suspicious. “He made us watch the film with him in his living room,” laughed Fleck. “Thankfully, he really liked it and said, ‘OK, you can have all of our music.’”

Turns out, it was kismet. “When we played the song ‘Lover’s Spit’ for Ryan, he was like, ‘Oh my God, who’s this band?’” said Boden. “He’d been listening to a burned Broken Social Scene CD in his car for the past two months and didn’t know what it was because it wasn’t labeled. It was meant to be!”

Twenty years on, “Half Nelson” feels like a product of a bygone time, one that benefitted from having the space it needed to find its audience. As the movie prepares for a 2027 dual disc re-release and a return to theatres, its remarkable journey hasn’t gone unappreciated by its creators.

“It wasn’t a huge blockbuster. It played really well in independent cinemas and the people who wanted to see it saw it. I’m not sure it works like that anymore,” said Boden. “So I’m really grateful for the experience we had with ‘Half Nelson.’”

Fleck echoed the sentiment: “It was our first and the one that allowed us to continue doing this. I love everything about the process of making that movie and think back on everything really fondly.”

entry.title: Cinematographers’ Favorite Festival Is All About AI This Year — but Artists Still Hate the Tech
entry.summary: TorunCamerimage kicked off with AI generated videos and remarks from a robot.
entry.content:
During the opening ceremony of the 34th ToruńCAMERIMAGE International Film Festival on Saturday, November 7, audience members saw a human replaced by a machine right in front of their eyes. The festival’s founder and artistic director Marek Żydowicz was invited to the stage, only for a robot to walk out in his place and begin addressing the audience and thanking sponsors.

Żydowicz took the stage a few moments later and joked that none of us are immune to the threat of AI and robots coming for our jobs. (The machine was Edward Warchocki, a humanoid robot “influencer” who has gone viral in Poland for videos in which it chases wild boars around Warsaw.) The stunt set a fitting tone for a festival that has devoted this edition to covering the film industry’s most controversial topic. Warchocki remained on stage for much of the opening ceremony, later joined by an actor in an “Inland Empire” rabbit costume who helped tee up an AI-generated video in which the rabbit symbolically opened the festival gates to the new technology. Anyone hoping for a boring, consensus-driven film festival immediately had their expectations adjusted.

Related Stories
‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards
Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release

A festival devoted to the technological craft of filmmaking is a fitting place for these discussions. ToruńCAMERIMAGE (formerly known as Camerimage before changing its name to include its Polish host city) is an annual homecoming for cinematographers. Directors of photography are treated like rockstars at the festival, and the entire profession makes an effort to descend upon Toruń each November to discuss their craft and party late into the night. The main competition screenings are crucial to the Best Cinematography Oscar race, with so much of the voting branch in one room. Panels and Q&As often focus on the specific technical details that the overwhelmingly below-the-line audience wouldn’t hear at other festivals. The job of a cinematographer is uniquely positioned at the intersection of art and technology, and the festival was right to assume that its audience would have a lot of thoughts about the topic.

ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 is taking a pluralistic approach to the subject by giving AI advocates and opponents equal time, and the programming appears more interested in stirring the pot and sparking discussion than taking a firm position. The festival gave an honorary award to Darren Aronofsky, who has founded an AI studio that works with Google DeepMind, yet also programmed Luca Guadagnino’s biting Sam Altman satire “Artificial” as its opening night film. The opening ceremony was interspersed with video clips featuring the likes of Aronofsky, Steven Spielberg, Gal Gadot, and Ben Affleck sharing views on AI that ranged from optimistic to paranoid. The message was clear: All opinions are welcome, but we can’t put off talking about AI.

Broadly speaking, directors have been more open to the technology than cinematographers — before “Artificial” screened, Guadagnino stressed that his film was driven more by opposition to the consolidation of wealth and power in a few individuals than AI itself. He explained that he simply sees AI as a neutral tool, though he described its current filmmaking applications as a “cheap” trend that he expects to fade with time in the same way that 3D did. And while Aronofsky avoided the topic in his award acceptance speech, a video message from him played during the opening ceremony saw him repeating his mantra that film has always been a technology-driven medium and AI is simply the latest tech innovation that storytellers need to embrace.

But the cinematographers in attendance have not shied away from the bleak reality that the technology is creating. The term “we’re fucked” has been thrown around a lot, and audience questions have been fiery. The program is filled with panels about AI’s influence on cinematography, many of which focus on the rise of “greybox” filmmaking. The technique, notably employed on Doug Liman’s upcoming “Bitcoin” movie and rapidly popping up on other projects, involves filming actors on a neutral background before using AI to add all the production design and lighting during post.

Nobody is denying the practicality of the rapidly improving technology, which eliminates logistical problems relating to weather and locations that have plagued filmmakers for as long as the art form has existed. But it fundamentally alters the role of a cinematographer, whose job has always been to use light and composition techniques to create images in camera. Cinematographers speak about directors asking them for the softest, most generic lighting on set — not because it looks the best, but because it provides the blankest canvas for changing things in post. Even if you’re still booking gigs as a cinematographer, are you even doing the same job if you’re no longer lighting each image?

Cinematography has always been an art form that’s easy to recognize but hard to describe. Countless moviegoers have walked out of theaters praising a film’s cinematography while having no idea what a director of photography actually does on set and how that job overlaps with other positions. A cinematographer’s job is to make images beautiful (or ugly, when the script calls for it) with their knowledge of light and camera equipment. But directors can theoretically frame their own shots, gaffers can light them, and colorists play an increasingly large role in shaping the final look of each image. A recurring topic at the festival has been the fear that new technologies could freeze cinematographers out of the process altogether.

At a debate titled “State of the Image,” Polish cinematographer Bartosz Nalazek was initially presented as the most pro-AI voice on the panel. He explained how he recently wrapped a major TV show that used greybox techniques for 40 percent of its scenes. His message was that cinematographers have to embrace and adapt to the technology in order to keep working. After he finished his opening statement, fellow cinematographer Arthur Reinhart, a two-time recipient of the festival’s Golden Frog award, asked a simple question: “Are you enjoying the work?”

Nalazek did not hesitate to respond. “Totally not,” he said. “It’s horrible, I’m brain-dead.” He went on to explain that while hybrid production is technically easier for cinematographers, moving so much of the artistry to post-production means that “an elevated camera operator could do it.”

The topic represents a seismic change to a constant that cinematographers could always take for granted: their status as the most technologically savvy person on set. Even as filmmaking tools shifted from film stock to digital cameras, DPs stayed employed and respected because they knew how to use those tools better than anyone else. Now, for the first time in history, technology threatens to be the force that pushes them out of the decision-making process.

“I think what made cinematographers become who we are is the leverage over technology and the creative input. When we were shooting on film, that leverage was tremendous because nobody knew how to do it except the cinematographers,” Nalazek said. “What worries me is that we have this feeling that our position is undoubtable and unchangeable. We have this feeling that the director should respect us, the producer should respect us. I think running on that thought is pretty dangerous. We’re kind of in a time where we have to prove our worth. And that’s sad.”

One advantage of having these conversations at such a technically-oriented festival is that the cinematographers are also honest about what AI isn’t doing. Criticisms are often preempted with the caveat that AI is a broad, loaded term — anyone who edits in DaVinci or uses biometric functions on cameras has technically been using AI tools for years. Cinematographers who have worked on greybox sets make it clear that hybrid AI films are not made by one guy typing prompts in a room by himself. It can be true that AI has shrunk crew sizes enough for the community to feel strained while still acknowledging that these projects often employ hundreds of traditional film workers. And speakers have at times pushed back against audience questions that blame all AI adoption on strawman arguments about greedy producers and execs who could afford to pay artists but simply don’t want to. But nuance doesn’t make the problem any less existential.

Nobody knows where things are going next, but there’s a deep sense that every option and idea should be on the table right now. Some cinematographers are making peace with the notion that traditional filmmaking will become a specialized niche product, akin to artisanal pottery or handmade furniture, rather than the norm for everyday entertainment. We’ll be making a luxury product for a smaller audience willing to pay for it, and we’ll have to charge them accordingly, the thinking goes. Others have floated the idea that the on-set cinematography work of setting up shots will become a lower-level, commoditized job. Directors will still need masterful artists like Roger Deakins to advise them on lighting and image composition, but that high-level work could become more of a post-production role.

The only idea that nobody is taking seriously is that there’s anything cinematographers can do to put the AI genie back in the bottle.

“Camerimage is a place where all the cinematographers from around the world are coming,” Reinhart said. “If we had a voice, then it should be coming from here, and I hope it will. But I am not very optimistic it will change anything.”

entry.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards
entry.summary: The CCA gave Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder's 'You Can See Everything' five prizes. 'Once Upon a Time in Harlem' also a big winner with three.
entry.content:
“You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim‘s phenomenally successful documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, swept the Critics Choice Association‘s documentary awards tonight, winning each of its five categories — including Best Documentary Feature. Ava DuVernay’s “14th,” which headed into the night with the most nominations (six), went home empty-handed.

In addition to the top prize, “You Can See Everything” won Best Director (Fielder and Oppenheimer), Best Cinematography (David Bolen), Best Editing (Adam Locke-Norton), and Best Music Score (Ari Balouzian).

Whether or not this is a harbinger of the film‘s Oscar chances is anybody’s guess. A24 is aggressively campaigning for “You Can See Everything” to score both Best Documentary and Best Picture nominations. If the film receives the latter, it would be the first documentary ever to do so. The CCA sweep certainly doesn’t hurt its prospects, but it’s not necessarily a predictor either — in the last 10 years, the CCA and Academy have only agreed on the best documentary twice (with “O.J.: Made in America” and “Summer of Soul”).

Related Stories
Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release
Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Thunders with $31.6 Million, Scoring the Biggest Debut Ever for a Live-Action, Foreign Language Film

Other winners tonight included David Greaves’ “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” which took home awards for Best First Documentary Feature, Best Historical Documentary and Best Archival Documentary, and Alex Gibney’s four-hour “Musk,” which won Best Biographical Documentary. John Wilson scored an award for Best Narration for his work as writer and performer on “A History of Concrete,” and Baz Luhrmann’s maximalist “EPiC: Elvis Presley in Concert” won Best Music Documentary.

The movie currently favored by many awards season pundits to take home the Best Documentary Oscar, “Naza,” won Best Political Documentary, and Best Science/Nature Documentary went to “Nuisance Bear.” Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin’s widely acclaimed “Everest: The Other Side” was awarded Best Sports Documentary.

entry.title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Hits $80 Million, Becoming A24’s Third-Biggest Domestic Release
entry.summary: 'You Can See Everything' has earned $80 million, making it A24's third-biggest domestic release.
entry.content:
“You Can See Everything,” an intimate look at Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has earned nearly $80 million at the domestic box office, becoming A24‘s third-highest-grossing release in North America. It bypasses “Everything Everywhere All at Once” and its $77 million haul to take its spot on the indie studio’s chart, and that film won the Oscar for Best Picture.

With $79.8 million stateside, “You Can See Everything” sits behind the summer blockbuster “Backrooms” ($197 million) and 2025’s “Marty Supreme” ($96 million) on the list of A24 releases. Other A24 films made more globally, with “Backrooms” earning more than $400 million, “Marty Supreme” grossing $192.4 million, and “Everything Everywhere All at Once” netting $147.9 million.

Related Stories
Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Thunders with $31.6 Million, Scoring the Biggest Debut Ever for a Live-Action, Foreign Language Film
Dylan Skolnick Returning as Co-Director of the Cinema Arts Centre Following Protests and Boycotts

However, “You Can See Everything” has yet to be released in most international markets. It’s unclear if Holmes’ fraud will resonate with moviegoers so far from Silicon Valley. It doesn’t matter if it doesn’t connect, because with a budget of $7 million, “You Can See Everything” is already wildly profitable. Its success means that Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the directing duo behind the doc, are now in high demand.

“You Can See Everything” also jumped ahead of “March of the Penguins” ($77 million) on the list of highest-grossing documentaries in North America. Variety reports that makes it the second highest-grossing doc behind Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which earned $119 million domestically. That doesn’t account for music documentaries like “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour” ($267.1 million) and “Michael Jackson’s This is It” ($268 million), which were far more popular.

A24 is on a hot streak. In addition to “Backrooms,” the indie studio has released hits like “The Drama” and “Primetime.” Its latest film, “Club Kid,” grossed an impressive $390,583 this weekend when it opened on six screens in New York and Los Angeles. That’s a per-screen average of $65,097. A24 acquired the drama about a hard-living gay man and his son out of the Cannes Film Festival, where it debuted to raves. The studio hopes to position the film and its writer, director, and star Jordan Firstman in the Oscar race.

entry.title: Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Thunders with $31.6 Million, Scoring the Biggest Debut Ever for a Live-Action, Foreign Language Film
entry.summary: 'Godzilla Minus Zero' broke box office records to become the biggest live-action foreign-language debut.
entry.content:
The year of unlikely box office smashes continues as “Godzilla Minus Zero” opened to a thunderous $31.6 million, shattering records to become the biggest North American debut for a live-action foreign language film in history. It easily toppled the previous benchmark established in 2002 by the wuxia epic “Hero,” which kicked off with $17.8 million. Globally, “Godzilla Minus Zero’s” haul stands at $63 million.

And it comes on the heels of a string of films that have defied conventional wisdom to resonate with moviegoers. Yes, the box office is still dominated by sequels and comic book movies like “Toy Story 5” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” but there’s been a lot more variety. Audiences have turned out in force for an original sci-fi adventure (“Project Hail Mary,” $684.6 million worldwide); a pair of low-budget horror films from 20-something auteurs with YouTube pedigree (“Obsession,” $524.3 million worldwide; “Backrooms,” $400.6 million worldwide); an adaptation of a Greek epic we were all forced to read in school (“The Odyssey,” $1.8 billion worldwide), and a three-hour documentary about a Silicon Valley cheat (“You Can See Everything,” $73.7 million and counting). Clearly, people are looking for something different.

Related Stories
Dylan Skolnick Returning as Co-Director of the Cinema Arts Centre Following Protests and Boycotts
Eric Bauza’s Final ‘Looney Tunes’ Performance Is ‘Daffy Season,’ Now in Theaters Ahead of ‘The Cat in the Hat’

In the case of “Godzilla Minus Zero,” it helped that the first film, 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” was an unexpected sleeper hit, grossing an impressive $57.1 million. But the first “Godzilla” opened to a mere $11.4 million, showing that the audience for the first monster movie grew on home entertainment. “Godzilla Minus Zero” is poised to bypass its predecessor to become the highest-grossing live-action Japanese movie in history. Once again, the film was directed by Takashi Yamazaki, who also worked on the special effects, produced by Japan’s Tojo, and distributed in the U.S. by GKids.

The success of “Godzilla Minus Zero” also demonstrates that subtitles are no barrier to box office success, something that Netflix and other streamers discovered with the popularity of local-language programming like “Squid Game,” “Money Heist,” and “Lupin.” The story at multiplexes is no different. U.S. audiences have filled auditoriums to watch “Parasite” ($53.8 million domestic),
“Ne Zha 2” ($23.2 million domestic), and “Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba – The Movie: Infinity Castle” ($136.9 million domestic). The outsized grosses for “Godzilla Minus Zero” probably mean we haven’t heard the last of the fire-breathing Kaiju.

The monster movie made quick work of its main competition, Warner Bros. Animation’s “The Cat in the Hat,” which stumbled with $20 million domestically and $30 million globally. The family film cost $92 million to produce and extends a string of misses for Warner Bros., which was recently purchased by Skydance. Insiders say that the studio has lost hundreds of millions of dollars on bombs like “Digger,” “Supergirl,” and “The Bride!” and “The Cat in the Hat” won’t do much to mop up all that red ink.
